source.citation: Palandri, J. L., Kharaka, Y. K. (2004). A compilation of rate parameters of water-mineral interaction kinetics for application to geochemical modeling. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 2004-1068.

transcription.from: the published report (PDF from pubs.usgs.gov, OFR_2004_1068.pdf), Tables 4, 6, 26, 31, 32, 33 and 34, read on the rendered pages 14, 15, 37 and 40 to 43; Tables 13, 15, 18, 23, 25, 27, 28, 29, 30, 35, 36 and 37 read on the rendered pages 24 to 45 twice, independently (200 and 300 dpi), and compared with the text layer, with no disagreement
transcription.note: The calcite acid and neutral parameters were typed in docstring examples of src/kinetics/rate_models.jl and in docs/src/manual/kinetics_syntax.md, as 10^log k rounded to four digits; they agree with the table. A dash in the report (no mechanism, or no parameter) is null here.

silica_rates.location: Table 4, p. 14 (quartz) and Table 6, p. 15 (amorphous silica and cristobalite, dissolution)
rows: quartz, geometric surface area (Tester et al. 1994)
quartz, BET surface area (Tester et al. 1994)

notes: log k is the decimal logarithm of the rate constant in mol m^-2 s^-1 at 25 C (for the acid mechanism, at pH 0); E is the Arrhenius activation energy; n is the reaction order with respect to H+ (acid and base) or to P(CO2) (carbonate). A base mechanism has a negative order in H+.
A is the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor of the report's equation (5), given in Tables 4 and 6 only; log k = log10 A - E/(ln(10) R 298.15 K) to the rounding of the tables.
Dawsonite, for which Table 33 gives only a neutral mechanism, is left out. The activation energies of magnesite are those of calcite, which the report assigns to it for want of data.

Table 4 prints the activation energy of the base mechanism of quartz as 108366 under a heading in kJ/mol; every other energy of the report is of order 10 to 100 kJ/mol, so the number is read as J/mol and stored as 108.366 kJ/mol. The log k of that row, -16.29, is what the pre-exponential factor of Knauss and Wolery (1988), 491, gives with that energy; with the factor the table prints, 10 (footnote i: adjusted from 491 to agree with Tester et al. 1994), it would be -17.98. Both are stored as printed, and the row is used through its log k.
Table 34 prints 0 for the activation energy of the neutral mechanism of gypsum, and the text above it (p. 42) says the data were insufficient to calculate it: stored as null, not as zero.
The quartz and amorphous silica rows differ in the surface area the rate is normalized by (geometric or BET, Table 4) or in the data set regressed (Table 6); the report does not single one out.

Tables 13 to 37 added here follow the conventions of the tables above: log k at 25 C and, for the acid mechanism, pH 0, in log mol m^-2 s^-1 (footnote a of each table); E in kJ/mol; n the order in H+ unless the column name says otherwise. A dash is null. Mineral names are lowercased; a qualifier taken from a footnote or added to keep row names unique is placed after a comma, as for dolomite above.
Table 13: the parameters of oligoclase, andesine, labradorite and bytownite are interpolated graphically between albite and anorthite (text, p. 16).

Table 13, albite: log k of the three mechanisms is that of the non-linear regression of Table 1 (p. 8: -10.16, -12.56, -15.60), while E and n are those of its linear regression (65.0, 69.8, 71.0; 0.457, -0.572); the report does not comment on the combination. The text (pp. 16-17) gives chemical affinity parameters p = 0.760 and q = 90.0 for albite, valid only near 300 C and pH 9; they are not part of Table 13 and are not stored.
Table 15 prints a single row without a mineral label; the name is taken from the caption.

Rows taken from Sverdrup (1990) have E computed in the report from two rate constants, at 8 and 25 C: leucite and the nepheline base mechanism (Table 18), fayalite (acid), almandine, grossular, andradite, staurolite and zoisite (acid) (Table 23), cordierite and tourmaline (Table 25), glaucophane, hornblende, riebeckite and tremolite (Table 27), glauconite (Table 28), lizardite (Table 30). Where the report tabulates the two constants (Tables 17, 20, 24), every one of the 19 E values is reproduced to the printed digit by E = R ln(10) (log k25 - log k8) / (1/281.15 K - 1/298.15 K).

Table 18, leucite: the acid and neutral log k (-6.00, -9.20) are exactly 3.00 above the log k at 25 C of Table 17 (-9.0, -12.2), although both tables state log mol m^-2 s^-1; in Tables 23 and 25 the log k at 25 C of Tables 20 and 24 is carried over unchanged. The base log k, -10.66, is neither Table 17's -10.8 nor 3 above it. Stored as printed.
Table 30, footnote d: the chlorite is clinochlore 14 Å.

Table 35: the acid mechanism carries two orders, with respect to H+ (footnote c, acid_n_H) and to Fe3+ (footnote d, acid_n_Fe3); the order of the neutral mechanism is with respect to O2 (footnote e, neutral_n_O2); the base order is with respect to H+. Footnote a defines k at pH 0 in mol m^-2 s^-1 only: the table does not state the scale (concentration, activity or pressure) of Fe3+ and O2 that k refers to. The acid order in H+ of pyrite and pyrrhotite is negative, as printed.
Table 35: the two pyrrhotite rows are distinguished by footnotes f (monoclinic) and g (hexagonal), and As2S3 by footnote h (amorphous); these qualifiers are carried in the row names.

Table 36: E = 250.0 kJ/mol comes from hydroxyapatite experiments at 25 and 28 C only, and the text (p. 44) warns that its uncertainty may be large; fluorapatite is given the hydroxyapatite E, and the neutral mechanism of both is a cut-off rate constant (rates not decreasing with pH above 7) with E set equal to the acid one.

Table 37: the log k of halite and of fluorite are far-from-equilibrium rate constants derived from data near equilibrium (saturation ratio 0.90 to 0.94 for halite, 0.40 for fluorite); the fluorite E is taken from a study other than its log k, and its neutral E equals the acid one (text, p. 45).

Tables 17, 20 and 24 (rate constants at 8 and 25 C from Sverdrup 1990, with orders, no activation energy) are inputs to Tables 18, 23 and 25 and are not transcribed. Table 1 (albite, p. 8, two regressions of the same data with chemical affinity) is not transcribed either; Table 13 holds the albite parameters the report retains.

Table 2 (p. 10), the regressions of the magnesite data of Pokrovsky and Schott (1999) that illustrate the method, is not transcribed: its non-linear row prints log k equal to log10 A in both mechanisms, which cannot reproduce Figure 2, and its acid activation energy, 14.5 kJ/mol, is not the 14.4 of calcite the text says it uses (the printed log k of the linear row follows from 14.4). Magnesite is in Table 33.
